# HTTP 301 vs 302

A 301 response tells the client the resource has moved permanently and it should use the new URL from now on, while a 302 tells it the move is temporary and it should keep using the original URL.

A 301 is a change-of-address card. A 302 is a detour sign during roadworks.

Many clients turn a redirected POST into a GET under either code, so use 308 (permanent) or 307 (temporary) when the method must stay the same, as it must for a webhook.

# Exponential Backoff

Exponential backoff is a retry policy in which a client waits longer after each failed attempt, usually doubling the delay, so a struggling service gets room to recover.

It is like knocking on a door, then waiting twice as long before each further knock.

A client that fails at 1s waits 2s, then 4s, then 8s, up to a cap. Backoff alone is not enough. Clients that failed at the same moment compute the same delays, so their retries arrive together in synchronized waves. Jitter breaks that up and is essential, not cosmetic. With full jitter, each client sleeps a random time between zero and the current cap.

# At-Least-Once Delivery

At-least-once delivery is a guarantee in which the sender retries a message until it sees an acknowledgement, so every message arrives, but a slow or lost acknowledgement makes it arrive more than once.

It is like a courier who keeps coming back with the parcel until someone signs for it. If you sign too slowly, you end up with two parcels.

A payment provider sent `charge.succeeded` for one charge. The handler took 34 seconds, the provider gave up at 30 and retried, and the customer got two receipt emails. No provider offers an "exactly-once" switch. The consumer has to tolerate duplicates.

Links: [[Idempotent Consumer]], [[Exponential Backoff]], [[Distributed Systems]]

# Idempotent Consumer

An idempotent consumer records the ID of every message it has handled and skips any message whose ID it has already seen, so a duplicate delivery has no further effect.

It is like a bouncer with a list of names already inside: someone who shows up twice is waved off the second time.

A webhook handler inserts each event ID into a `processed_events` table with a unique constraint and skips the work when the insert conflicts. Combined with [[At-Least-Once Delivery]], this gives "effectively once" processing. It is the [[Idempotency Key]] pointed the other way: the key protects the provider from our retries, and this table protects us from theirs. One limit remains: a side effect that leaves the system, such as a sent email, can't be rolled back, so the window between doing the work and recording the ID still matters.

Links: [[At-Least-Once Delivery]], [[Idempotency Key]], [[Data Systems in Practice]], [[Distributed Systems]]

# Invariant

An invariant is a condition that stays true for the whole lifetime of a system or data structure, no matter which operations run.

It is like the rule in double-entry bookkeeping that debits equal credits: every individual entry may change, but the balance between them never breaks.

"An account balance never goes negative" and "at most one node holds the lock" are invariants. So is "the lint warning count on main never increases from one commit to the next", which a [[Ratchet (Engineering)]] enforces. Invariants are worth stating separately from the checks that enforce them. When two pull requests both edit the baseline file, that is a merge conflict, not a broken invariant.

Links: [[Ratchet (Engineering)]], [[Distributed Systems]]
